source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives, Table 2
finding: Table 2 re-read. Four partitions (analogy type, distractor type). Models are good when surface and structure agree and collapse when they conflict. This fixes the ARN numbers (gap 7).
numbers: Partition averages over 9 models plus SBERT: near analogy vs far distractor 76.9, near vs near 73.2, far vs far 45.3, far analogy vs near distractor 33.9, overall 57.3. Humans 98.6/97.2/96.8/91.4, overall 96.0. Far-analogy mean: humans 94.1 vs models 39.6 (below the 50% chance level). Near-analogy mean: humans 97.9 vs models 75.0. GPT-4 overall 68.1; SBERT 42.3 overall and 1% when a far analogy must beat a near distractor.
quote: most challenging partition, where models needed to prioritize far analogies over near distractors
limits: Zero-shot, temperature 0, two-way choice (chance 50). Column order inferred from the text because the table layout is garbled. Models are 2023 era (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2, FlanT5, UnifiedQA, Macaw).
agent_relevance: Choosing by surface similarity is worse than chance when structure and surface disagree. A code check that compares relations, not words, is the right guard.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: few-shot and CoT sections
finding: Same paper: solved demonstrations help far analogies by close to 10 absolute points, and near-analogy demonstrations act as hints.
numbers: Text: gain on far analogies close to 10 absolute points with demonstrations. Error analysis: GPT-4 rationales were mostly based on high-level messages.
limits: Exact per-model few-shot table not extracted. Demonstrations were chosen at random.
agent_relevance: Showing worked structural mappings may help more than any added checklist, but this needs a direct test.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? Tables 5, 7, 8
finding: Qin ran the accuracy-controlled test (gap 3). Accuracy of the self-written examples, not their relevance, drives the gain on math. Fixed, checked examples written once beat per-query relevant ones.
numbers: GPT-3.5, MATH: share of correct self-generated examples 62.0 (relevant), 72.0 (N/A), 86.0 (random same-domain). GSM8K+MATH average: relevant 52.4, N/A 55.8, random-same 55.7, random-diff 55.2, random-bio 54.9, fixed verified math examples (ICL-math) 56.3, fixed verified bio examples (ICL-bio) 56.4. GSM8K: relevant 71.5, ICL-bio 77.9. Using GPT-4's accurate answers (GPT4-Calibration) beat plain ICL for all methods; random wrong answers were always worst. Open models: Llama-3-8B relevant 69.5, N/A 72.3, ICL-math 75.8, ICL-bio 76.8; Llama-2-70B relevant 45.1, N/A 51.4, ICL-math 55.5.
limits: Mostly GPT-3.5 and math. On BBH relevant examples did help (+1.3 points over no-example). Accuracy was checked by hand on 50 samples per method.
agent_relevance: Text the model writes is only as good as its accuracy. Any step that makes the agent write analogues should have code or a checker verify the analogue, otherwise skip it.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Table 4: relevance scores
finding: Relevance was measured by embedding similarity between generated examples and the query, so relevant examples truly were closer.
numbers: Mean cosine similarity (GSM8K/MATH/avg): relevant 0.54/0.41/0.48, N/A 0.19/0.28/0.24, random-same 0.30/0.20/0.25, random-diff 0.15/0.10/0.13, random-bio 0.06/0.11/0.09, oracle (nearest training items) 0.65/0.63/0.64.
limits: Embedding similarity is a surface measure. It says nothing about causal fit (Hesse) or a critical disanalogy (Bartha).
agent_relevance: The study cannot say whether a causally relevant but inaccurate example hurts more. The Hesse/Bartha view predicts it would; there is no data.

source: Calvo Figueras and Agerri (2025) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation, sections 3.2 and 6.2
finding: Reference critical questions were built from Walton (2008) scheme templates plus Llama-3-70B and then hand-labelled. Zero-shot LLMs without templates stay near 57% Useful. Systems built for the task did about 10 points better.
numbers: 11 LLMs zero-shot: none above 57% Useful on average (claude-3-5-sonnet 56.21, gpt-4o 52.29, o4-mini 53.27 on one metric, mean of 3 runs). Task-specific systems (Calvo Figueras et al. 2025 shared task) 'nearly 10 points higher'. 22.4 reference questions per intervention on average. Annotator agreement 0.54 in the last round. Judge-ranking correlation with human ranking: Pearson 0.86 (Claude reference-based), 0.80 (Gemma).
quote: no model generates more than 57% of Useful CQs on average
limits: Data is political debate and online text, not scientific analogies; argument from analogy is one scheme among several. Useful labels are subjective (agreement 0.54).
agent_relevance: Template-guided question lists plausibly add about 10 points over free generation. This supports a fixed question list in the agent but is not a test on analogy arguments.

source: Puranam, Sen and Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs Help Improve Analogical Reasoning For Strategic Decisions?
finding: Humans (n=199) and GPT-4 (60 runs) solved business problems that needed a source story. With a hint GPT-4 always found the right analogy but could not tell right from wrong source; humans were precise but missed most.
numbers: With hint, GPT-4 Radiation: TP 15, FN 0, FP 14, TN 1 (precision about 0.52). GPT-4 Dolphin: TP 15, FP 15, TN 0 (precision 0.50). Humans Radiation: TP 12, FN 34, FP 6, TN 40 (precision 0.67, recall 0.26). Without hint GPT-4 never used the correct story (precision and recall 0); humans Radiation precision 0.42 recall 0.06, Dolphin precision 1.00 recall 0.22. GPT-4 solved the problems more often than humans overall.
quote: LLMs as broad analogy generators, while humans act as critical evaluators
limits: Two source pairs, one model (GPT-4), students as humans. Few distinct items.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a test of the matching step: the model accepts surface-matching sources. A causal-alignment check (Hesse's causal condition) is what is missing. Indirect support for gap 8.

source: Xiang et al. (2026) Grounding Before Generalizing: How AI Differs from Humans in Causal Transfer
finding: OpenLock: models discover Common Cause (cc) and Common Effect (ce) structures and then must transfer. 2026 frontier models mostly do not transfer causal structure; humans do. Partly answers gaps 2 and 4.
numbers: Humans N=80 (Edmonds 2018): success 65.0%, attempts 19.4/22.0. Text-only Exp 1 success cc/ce: GPT-5.2 100/66.7, Claude-4.5-Sonnet 67.7/86.7, Gemini-3-Flash 100/100, DeepSeek-V3.2 96.7/86.2. Exp 2 attempts baseline to transfer: humans 20.66 to 13.85 (+33.0%, p<.001); GPT-5.2 15.77 to 17.43 (-10.5%, p=.266); Claude-4.5 15.74 to 12.92 (+17.9%, p=.090); Gemini-3-Flash 9.08 to 7.33 (+19.3%, p=.003); DeepSeek-V3.2 19.35 to 17.32 (+10.5%, p=.089). 30 agents per structure per model. GPT-5.2 favoured cc (11.8 vs 19.7 attempts, p<.001); humans showed no cc/ce difference (p=.207).
limits: Only Gemini-3-Flash transfers significantly. Interactive game, not judging analogy arguments. Page read through a summariser (HTML fetch), model effort settings not seen.
agent_relevance: Models treat causal direction differently while humans do not. A typed mapping that stores causal direction in code is a plausible fix, but no study tested it.

source: Chen, Wang and Wang (2026) ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning, Table 2
finding: A far-analogy benchmark (real-world objects mapped to grid transformations) shows a large gap to humans for GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.5 and Grok 4.1 Fast. Extends gap 4 to the newest models.
numbers: Total pass@3, with typo / without typo: GPT 5.2 51.20 / 48.33; Gemini 3 Pro 43.06 / 29.19; Grok 4.1 Fast 24.88 / 18.66; Claude Opus 4.5 8.61 / 7.18. Humans pass@1 68.96 / 58.35 on average, 96 / 93.5 when at least 2 participants agree. ConceptSIR solved 9 of 17 hard tasks (52.9%), one run each, no baseline on that subset.
limits: LLM pass@3 vs human pass@1: not like for like. Thinking settings not stated in what I read. ConceptSIR gain has no baseline.
agent_relevance: Far analogy is not solved by 2026 frontier models. Do not assume analogy is reliable; keep code checks on mappings.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in LLMs, version history and text search
finding: Only one version exists (v1, 21 Nov 2024). It tests GPT models only. The reference list cites an analysis of OpenAI o1 (arXiv 2410.01792) but the paper does not test o1 or any reasoning model.
numbers: Text search of the PDF for o1, o3, reasoning model, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek: one hit, the reference.
limits: Absence is from a text search of the PDF.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open for counterfactual letter-string variants: I found no 2025-2026 reasoning-model run of Lewis-Mitchell style variants.

source: arXiv title/abstract searches, Nov 2026 (argument from analogy; analogical arguments; letter-string; analogical reasoning list)
finding: Negative search result. 'Argument from analogy' + language models: 0 hits. 'Analogical arguments': no relevant AI paper. 'Letter-string' + LLM: 4 hits. A 49-result analogical-reasoning list: none tests Hesse or Bartha criteria.
numbers: Counts: argument-from-analogy query 0 results; letter-string query 4 results (2411.14215, 2411.02348, 2511.00763, 2609.16793); analogical reasoning list 49 results, 44 read.
limits: arXiv search only. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API were rate limited; WebSearch budget was spent. Philosophy journals are not on arXiv.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (Hesse or Bartha checklist on LLMs) still has no study. Any such test must be run in our own harness.

source: Available but Unclaimed: An Empirical Study of Human-AI Synergy (2026), letter-string subset
finding: 535 participants answered 40 items (matrix, rotation, syllogism, letter-string) alone or with one of four 2026 LLM assistants. On letter-string items the advice was right 84.6% of the time but humans over-followed wrong advice.
numbers: Letter-string, 3,384 classified trials: advice correct 0.846, deference 0.751, overreliance (followed wrong advice) 0.482, realized synergy -0.153 (95% CI -0.218 to -0.090), synergy capture 0.484. Battery level, assistant alone: Gemini 3.6 Flash 0.761, Claude Opus 4.8 0.735, Kimi K3 0.730, GPT-5.6 Luna 0.713; unaided humans 0.528.
limits: Standard letter-string items, not counterfactual variants. Per-model letter-string accuracy not on the page I read.
agent_relevance: Frontier 2026 models solve standard letter-string items well (advice 84.6% correct). The failure that matters is on altered alphabets, which this study did not test. Gap 4 is half closed: standard items easy, variants unknown.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in LLMs (AAAI 2026)
finding: LLMs encode relations in mid-to-upper layers but often fail to apply them to new entities. Patching hidden states at key tokens partly improves transfer. Abstract only.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only. Models not named in what I read.
agent_relevance: The failure is in applying a relation, not in having it. This supports an explicit relation-to-entity mapping step.

source: McGovern et al. (2026) When Models Know More Than They Say: Probing Analogical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Probing beats prompting for rhetorical analogies in open models; for narrative analogies both are similar and low. Abstract only.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
agent_relevance: Narrative (causal) analogy judgment is hard even when read from inside the model, so a prompt rubric alone is unlikely to fix it.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors (ICLR 2024)
finding: Answer-position bias is general: 20 LLMs on 3 benchmarks prefer certain option labels, mostly from a label-token prior. A permutation-based fix (PriDe) reduces it. Abstract only.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks. No effect sizes on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; not on analogy items.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the Lewis-Mitchell order effect (GPT-4 0.89 first slot vs 0.61 second in WHL data) fits a general bias. Swapping order in code and voting is a cheap generic fix.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024), answer order and paraphrase sections (re-read)
finding: The story set is still the 18 stories of Webb et al. I found no larger story set with an order-swap test, so gap 6 is not answered at scale.
numbers: 18 story problems in both orderings; GPT-4 shows an order bias, humans none; paraphrasing the correct target lowers GPT-4 more than humans (humans saw 6 problems).
limits: Small item count; the authors say the paraphrase effect is not clearly significant.
agent_relevance: Use order-swap and paraphrase checks as a cheap robustness check, not as a proven fix.

source: Bartha, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, sections 3.3.3, 3.5.2, 3.6.1 (full HTML read)
finding: Full text read. 'Causal condition' and 'No-essential-difference condition' are Hesse's; 'Prior Association' and 'Potential for Generalization' are Bartha's. SEP says Hesse defines 'essential' only as 'causally closely related to the known positive analogy' and gives no theory of degree of support.
numbers: Hesse's own test case: the fluid-flow analogy for heat conduction was good until heat was found not to be conserved, then became unacceptable. Franklin's lightning list had 12 shared particulars and no known causal link yet stays plausible. Galileo's moon mountains: Norton's 'fact of the analogy' is that shadows arise the same way on Earth and Moon. On Norton's theory, for most analogical arguments (Clay pots, Life on other planets) there are no useful evaluation criteria. Rectangles and boxes show Hesse's essential-difference rule is too strict.
quote: Absent an inferential context, it is impossible to evaluate the importance or 'essentiality'
limits: Secondary source; Bartha wrote both the SEP entry and the 2010 book, so it is not an independent check. Hesse 1966 and Bartha 2010 not opened. Canals case not found in the SEP text.
agent_relevance: Gaps 8 and 10. A code test of essential difference needs a definition the agent can apply, but SEP says essentiality depends on the use of the analogy, so it cannot be a fixed list.

source: Bartha, SEP, section 4.1 on determination rules (Davies and Russell)
finding: Determination rules give a deductive justification but are rarely available. SEP says drug tests on animals are run without knowing all relevant attributes, so neither limiting scope nor justifying a rule is realistic there.
numbers: Form Q = F(P1..Pm). Example: used-car value from year, make, mileage, condition, colour, accident history. No count of how often real tasks have a known determinant set exists in the source.
limits: Conceptual argument, no frequency data. Gap 5 is answered only in principle.
agent_relevance: A code check for determinant sets will fire only on closed domains (pricing, lookup tables, physics formulas). On open tasks expect unknown determinants and fall back to soft flags.

source: Bartha, SEP, sections 3.5.2 and 4.3: scope of the articulation model
finding: Bartha's criteria in simplified form need a non-trivial positive analogy and no known critical disanalogy, and justify only prima facie plausibility, not degree of probability. SEP names two worries: the symmetry principle reading, and that the model may be too vague or too permissive.
numbers: Method steps: articulate the prior association (for Rectangles and boxes, a specific proof for rectangles), list the critical features (assumptions of the proof), check whether any lacks a target analogue.
limits: Philosophical argument. No empirical test of the model's reliability exists in the source.
agent_relevance: The model's output is a go/no-go for 'worth investigating', which fits an agent step that decides whether to test an analogy, not whether to believe it.
